Fischer had opened 1.e4 almost all his life, but two games ago he switched to 1.c4 and beat Spassky with it. He plays it again here, and the game reaches your line. Play your line, then try to find Fischer's moves.

Spassky died in 2025, aged 88.

column3: Svidler resigned after 30.c4: he can't hold d6 and h7 at once. Polgar had taken the Marshall's pawn, survived the attack by pushing the queen back and trading pieces, and then won with a pin. Peter Leko won the tournament. That autumn Polgar became the first woman to play in a world championship tournament, in San Luis. She retired from competitive chess in 2014 and works to bring chess into schools.

column14: Chess Olympiad, Tromsø, 2014: Latvia against Lithuania, top board. Alexei Shirov, born in Riga, is famous for wild attacking chess; his best games are collected in a book called Fire on Board. In 1998 he beat Kramnik to earn a world title match with Kasparov, a match that was never played. Here, against Lithuania's Sarunas Sulskis, he goes for the Fried Liver, your line: a knight sacrificed on f7 to drag Black's king into the open. Play your line, then find Shirov's moves.

The king in the middle
column5: Black is a rook up, but his king is on d6 with your knight on d5, bishop on c4 and queen on f3 around it. The king should have hidden: 11...Qh4 hits f2 and keeps Black on top. Now every pawn move that opens a line helps you. Which one?

column4: Open the lines
column5: d4 opens two lines at once: the c1 bishop's diagonal to g5 and h6, and the e-file for your rook. The material doesn't matter while Black's king stands in the centre.

column4: The skewer
column5: Qc6+ drove the king to e7, on the same diagonal as the queen on d8. Bg5+ checks the king, and when it moves, the bishop takes the queen.

column3: Sulskis resigned after 28.Rxg6: ...Kxg6 loses the d7 rook to Qe6+, and anything else lets the attack go on. It was 9.a3 that made the game: Shirov gave a rook to keep Black's king in the middle, and one slip, 11...Kd6 instead of 11...Qh4, was enough. Shirov played on for Latvia and Spain for many years, and he still plays the sharpest openings he can find.

Answer the lever
column5: White's f4 hit e5 and threatened f5, trapping your e6 bishop. ...f5 answers a lever with a lever: the f-file opens for your rooks, and your knight gets f5.

column4: A pawn in the throat

column4: Mate threat or recapture?
column5: White's queen and knight threaten Qxh7 mate, but White has left a piece on c3 to be taken. When your opponent makes a threat instead of taking back, look for a defence that comes with a gain of its own. Can you find it?

column4: Covered, with a follow-up

column3: White resigned after 23.Rf1: Black's queen on g3, the bishop on f5 and the pawn on e3 are all aimed at the king. Filippov's ...d4 gave him space in the centre, ...f5 opened the f-file, and when White chose a mate threat over a simple recapture, ...Bf5 and ...h6 turned White's attackers into targets. A good model for your ...d4 line: the d4 pawn gives you space, and ...e5 and ...f5 are the levers that follow.

column14: Sinquefield Cup, Saint Louis, 2015, round 6. Hikaru Nakamura, rated 2814, is the world's leading King's Indian player at the top level, and he plays it against anyone. Wesley So, who had just switched from the Philippines to the US federation, goes for the main line, your line: White attacks on the queen's side, Black on the king's side, and it becomes a race. Play your line, then find Nakamura's moves.

Out of play
column5: A knight on the edge is a knight out of play. The a3 knight is cut off from the centre and from the king's side, where the game will be decided. Black's next move takes c4 from it. Can you find it?

column4: The pawn breaker
column5: ...f3 gives a pawn to open lines at White's king: the f-file for your rook, and the e4 pawn loses its guard.

column4: Knight in
column5: ...Nxe4 gives material back to get at the king. Taking it with the f-pawn opens the f-file to your rook. The attack is now worth more than any piece.

column4: A forced mate
column5: After ...Qh6, Black has a forced mate. The king will be driven from h3 to g4, f5 and finally g6.

column3: The game ended in mate: 39...Qg5, with White's king on g6. So had spent the game on the queen's side, but the a3 knight was out of play when the King's Indian storm broke through with ...f3 and ...Nxe4. The win made Nakamura the live world number two. Levon Aronian won the tournament. So won the Sinquefield Cup himself the next year, and Nakamura went on to become the world's top blitz player and a hugely popular streamer.
